newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS-US investors still see value in Europe.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-US investors still see value in Europe.

text.p: While bets on European economic and monetary union have already created big rallies in second-tier European government bond markets, U.S. investors say those instruments still offer value.

"I still see some more value in Europe -- maybe in some of the higher yielding markets like Spain or Italy or Sweden," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

Feinman noted a general notion that the proposed Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is proceeding and said that "even if some countries don't get in on the first round, a lot of them will get in on the second round.

"It looks like (EMU) will come to pass and if countries like Italy, Spain and Sweden become part of one big bloc, they will have some of the same monetary policy credibility associated with them that Germany now has," Feinman said.
The inflation premiums still reflected in the government bond yields of some of these countries will shrink, he said.
That's because the proposed fiscal restrictions that would be a part of the EMU will make it hard for these nations to inflate their currencies, analysts said.
Keith Woodfin, currency analyst at Foreign Exchange Analytics, said European government bonds seem to keep going higher even when fundmentals threaten to reverse them.

"Everything has been very optimistic and money continues to flow into Italy and Spain basically on the belief that the governments have the political willpower to sweep aside structural deficits," said Woodfin.
That belief is not just based on talk, Woodfin said.
"You are seeing lower inflation in Italy and Spain and a commitment to fiscal austerity," he said.

"It's the same story in Sweden," said Woodfin. "They're not making quite the push that Italy and Spain are to join the EMU but you do have falling interest rates. The economic cycles are really converging."
Julie Grandstaff, vice president of global fixed-income at Bailard Biehl and Kaiser, said the tendency of the convergence trade would be to take investors out of the German market.
"From a long-term perspective, if monetary union goes through, Germany will underperform," said Grandstaff.
But Grandstaff said in the near-term, the convergence plays in the "peripheral markets" of Italy, Spain and Sweden have been overdone.
"There's no risk at all built into current prices," she said. "They are vulnerable to any news that would set them off the EMU track."
Grandstaff said of the higher yielding government bond markets, Sweden still offers the most potential value. The status of Sweden's entry into the EMU probably is the most precarious, she said.

Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, in a newspaper article written jointly with Social Democratic party secretary Ingela Thalen, said on Tuesday that the country could not put off a decision on whether it would participate in the EMU. The two called for an open debate on the issue of whether Sweden would join the EMU.
